subject: Chemistry
title: Disaccharides: Glycosidic Linkages, Reducing Status, & Invert Sugar
topics: 3. Disaccharide Structure & The Glycosidic Bond (Ether Linkage via Anomeric Carbon Condensation)
3.1 Disaccharide Comparison Matrix: Sucrose, Maltose, & Lactose
Sucrose: α-D-Glc-(1→2)-β-D-Fru, Both Anomeric Carbons Locked (NON-REDUCING SUGAR, No Mutarotation)
Maltose: α-D-Glc-(1→4)-α-D-Glc, Free C-1 Anomeric -OH (REDUCING SUGAR, Exhibits Mutarotation)
Lactose: β-D-Gal-(1→4)-α-D-Glc, Free C-1 Anomeric -OH (REDUCING SUGAR, Exhibits Mutarotation)
3.2 Inversion of Cane Sugar: Hydrolysis of Dextrorotatory Sucrose (+66.5°) to Levorotatory Invert Sugar (-19.85°)
quickSummary: Disaccharides are formed by glycosidic ether bonds. Sucrose [α-D-Glc-(1→2)-β-D-Fru] has both anomeric carbons locked and is a NON-REDUCING sugar (fails Fehling's/Tollens'). Maltose [α-(1→4)] and Lactose [β-(1→4)] have a free C-1 anomeric -OH and are REDUCING sugars. Hydrolysis of dextrorotatory sucrose (+66.5°) yields equimolar glucose (+52.7°) and fructose (-92.4°), producing levorotatory Invert Sugar (-19.85°).
summary: Master glycosidic linkages, reducing vs non-reducing disaccharides, and the inversion of cane sugar.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
DISACCHARIDE COMPARISON
                                      │
     ┌──────────────────┬─────────────┴─────────────┬──────────────────┐
     ▼                  ▼                           ▼                  ▼
  SUCROSE (Cane Sugar)  MALTOSE (Malt Sugar)        LACTOSE (Milk Sugar)
  ├── $\alpha$-D-Glc-(1$\to$2)-$\beta$-D-Fru           ├── $\alpha$-D-Glc-(1$\to$4)-$\alpha$-D-Glc      ├── $\beta$-D-Gal-(1$\to$4)-$\alpha$-D-Glc
  ├── **Both Anomeric Locked**  ├── Free C-1 Anomeric       ├── Free C-1 Anomeric
  └── **NON-REDUCING SUGAR**    └── **REDUCING SUGAR**      └── **REDUCING SUGAR**
conceptBreakdown.content: Disaccharides consist of two monosaccharide units joined by a Glycosidic Bond. In Sucrose, both anomeric carbons are engaged in the bond, eliminating free hemiacetal/hemiketal groups, rendering it non-reducing. Maltose and Lactose retain a free anomeric carbon at C-1 on one ring, making them reducing sugars.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 3.2 Inversion of Cane Sugar (Sucrose)
conceptBreakdown.title: 3.2 Inversion of Cane Sugar (Sucrose)
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
INVERSION OF SUGAR MECHANICS:

$$\text{Sucrose } (+66.5^\circ) + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+ \text{ / Invertase}} \text{D-(+)-Glucose } (+52.7^\circ) + \text{D-(-)-Fructose } (-92.4^\circ)$$

$$\text{Net Optical Rotation of Invert Sugar} = \frac{+52.7^\circ + (-92.4^\circ)}{2} = \mathbf{-19.85^\circ \text{ (Levorotatory)}}$$

• Optical rotation inverts from dextrorotatory (+) to levorotatory (-) because fructose levorotation (-92.4°) dominates over glucose dextrorotation (+52.7°).
conceptBreakdown.content: The resulting equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose is called Invert Sugar. Because it contains free open-chain forms of glucose and fructose, Invert Sugar is a powerful reducing sugar.

quickRevision: Invert sugar has net optical rotation of -19.85° (Levorotatory).
